transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started. As you all know, we have a preliminary-injunction hearing in three weeks, and I need to approve our response strategy before the motion papers are finalized. Before I sign off on anything, I need each of you to put your cards on the table — any material evidence you've uncovered, any business constraints I should be aware of, and any proposed filing commitments you think we need to make. I don't want surprises after we've already filed. Who wants to go first?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I'll go first, Marisol. I have some significant developments to report from the forensic review. After the strategy-memo cutoff, I received and began reviewing a forensic image that was delivered to us. I found material evidence that has not yet been incorporated into the motion outline, and I believe it changes what we should be requesting in our filing. I'd like to lay this out for the group before we finalize anything.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: Before Ethan gets into the forensic details, I want to flag a business constraint from the client side that directly affects what we should be requesting in any injunction. In this week's client call, I confirmed that the client will only support an injunction if it includes a 30-day customer-transition period for existing hosted customers and does not shut down the customer-facing service during that period. That's a hard line from the client, and I think it's critical everyone hears this before we lock in our filing strategy.

transcript.text: Marisol, here's what I found. In the forensic image delivered after the strategy-memo cutoff, I located the former employee's signed confidentiality agreement — that's a critical document we didn't previously have in our possession. More importantly, the logs show that 4,800 files were copied to an external drive, and those files include source code and deployment scripts. This is direct, concrete evidence of the scale of the taking. These supplemental findings have not yet been added to the motion outline. Given the signed agreement and the volume and nature of the files copied, I'm recommending that our motion include a request for an expedited forensic inspection of the competitor's systems, and that we file a supplemental-evidence submission to get these findings on the record before the hearing.

transcript.text: Ethan, that's compelling evidence, and the client will want to hear about the signed agreement and the scale of the file copying. But I want to make sure we're thinking through how your proposed expedited forensic inspection interacts with the client's constraint. If we're asking the court to order an inspection of the competitor's systems, we need to be careful about how that request is scoped — the client's priority is protecting existing hosted customers and maintaining service continuity during any transition period. An inspection order that could be read to authorize an immediate shutdown or service interruption would be a non-starter for them. I'd suggest we frame any inspection request as narrowly tailored to the allegedly misappropriated materials, with explicit carve-outs that preserve the competitor's ability to continue serving existing customers during the 30-day transition window. That way we get the evidence we need without contradicting the client's hard line. Marisol, can we make sure the motion language reflects both the supplemental evidence and the customer-service constraint as we move forward?
